## In 60 seconds

Radiofrequency (RF) ablation heats tissue with electric current. The generator drives current from
the catheter tip to a large patch on the skin. Near the small tip the current is crowded into a
small volume, so that is where the tissue heats; half of the heat is made within one electrode
radius of the tip surface. Heat then spreads outward by conduction and is carried away by blood.
Tissue that stays hot enough for long enough is injured for good and stops conducting. Power,
contact force, time and the fall in impedance are what a mapping system can show during an
application. Each is an input to, or a clue about, the lesion; none of them measures it.

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $I$ current (A). $\sigma$ electrical conductivity of tissue (S/m).
$r_0$ electrode radius (m). $r$ distance from the centre of the electrode (m). $J$ current density
(A/m²). $q$ power density, the heat made per unit volume (W/m³). $T$ temperature (°C), $T_b$ blood
and body temperature. $k$ thermal conductivity (W/(m·K)). $\rho$ density (kg/m³) and $c$ specific
heat (J/(kg·K)). $F$ contact force and $P$ generator power. $t$ time (s).

### Where the current goes and where the heat is made

At the frequencies used for RF ablation, 300 kHz to 1 MHz, tissue can be treated as purely
resistive because displacement currents are negligible, so models solve a quasi-static (Laplace)
problem for the voltage [@berjano2006]. Model the tip as a sphere of radius $r_0$ in a large,
uniform volume of tissue, with the return patch far away. The current leaves the sphere evenly in
all directions, and the same current $I$ crosses every sphere of radius $r$, so the current density
is

$$
J(r) = \frac{I}{4\pi r^2}, \qquad r \ge r_0
$$ {#eq-m27-current-density}

Resistive (Joule) heating per unit volume is $J^2/\sigma$:

$$
q(r) = \frac{J^2}{\sigma} = \frac{I^2}{16\pi^2\sigma\, r^4}
$$ {#eq-m27-power-density}

Heating falls as the fourth power of distance. Doubling the distance from the centre cuts it
sixteen-fold. Integrating $q$ over the shell between $r_0$ and $r$ gives the share of all tissue
heating made inside radius $r$:

$$
\frac{P(r_0 < r' < r)}{P_{\text{total}}} = 1 - \frac{r_0}{r}
$$ {#eq-m27-power-fraction}

Half of the heat is made between $r_0$ and $2r_0$, that is, within one electrode radius of the tip
surface. Tissue farther away is heated mostly by conduction from this thin shell.

The same integral gives the resistance the tissue presents to the generator. Adding thin shells in
series, each of thickness $dr$ and area $4\pi r^2$:

$$
R_s = \int_{r_0}^{\infty} \frac{dr}{4\pi r^2 \sigma} = \frac{1}{4\pi\sigma r_0}
\quad\text{(sphere)}, \qquad
R_s = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma r_0}
\quad\text{(hemisphere on an insulating flat face)}
$$ {#eq-m27-spreading}

The hemisphere carries the same current through half the area at every radius, so its resistance
doubles. This spreading resistance near the tip dominates the tissue part of the circuit: most of
the voltage drop, and most of the heating, happen close to the electrode.

A real tip is not buried in uniform tissue. Part of it touches the wall and part sits in blood,
which has a different conductivity, so the current divides between the two; how much reaches the
wall depends on contact and on the two conductivities (values: `TODO(source)`).

**Key takeaways**

- Current density falls as $1/r^2$ and heating as $1/r^4$; half the heat is made within one
  electrode radius of the tip surface.
- The spreading resistance $1/(4\pi\sigma r_0)$ near the tip dominates the tissue's share of the
  circuit.

### The heat balance: the bioheat equation

Temperature follows a balance of four terms. Pennes wrote it for perfused tissue [@pennes1948]:

$$
\rho c\, \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot\left(k \nabla T\right) + q - \omega_b \rho_b c_b \left(T - T_b\right)
$$ {#eq-m27-bioheat}

From left to right: heat stored, heat conducted, heat made by the current, and heat carried away by
blood flowing through the tissue at perfusion rate $\omega_b$ (1/s), with blood density $\rho_b$ and
specific heat $c_b$. Cooling at the surfaces enters as boundary conditions: models represent blood
flowing over the wall with a convective heat-transfer coefficient at the tissue–blood interface, and
an internally cooled electrode with a fixed temperature [@berjano2006].

**A steady state you can solve by hand.** Keep spherical symmetry, constant properties and no
perfusion, and wait until nothing changes. With $q$ from @eq-m27-power-density, the equation
becomes $k\,r^{-2}\,(r^2 T')' = -q$. Integrating twice and requiring $T \to T_b$ far away:

$$
T(r) = T_b + \frac{A}{r} - \frac{B}{r^2}, \qquad B = \frac{I^2}{32\pi^2 \sigma k}
$$ {#eq-m27-steady-temperature}

The constant $A$ is set by the condition at the tip, for example a fixed interface temperature
$T_e$. The $A/r$ term is pure conduction from a hot sphere; the $-B/r^2$ term adds the heat made
inside the tissue. Haines and Watson measured a hyperbolic fall of tissue temperature with distance
in an isolated-tissue model, close to a model of this kind [@haines1989].

**Where is the lesion edge?** If injury happens wherever the tissue reaches a temperature $T_L$,
the lesion edge is the isotherm $T(r_L) = T_L$. Keeping only the conduction term, with the
interface held at $T_e$:

$$
r_L = r_0\,\frac{T_e - T_b}{T_L - T_b}
$$ {#eq-m27-isotherm}

so the lesion radius is proportional to the electrode radius. Haines and colleagues found exactly
this proportionality when they held the interface temperature constant and varied the electrode
radius [@haines1990].

**How fast heat spreads.** Without the source, the heat equation spreads a point of heat as a
Gaussian, $\exp\!\left(-x^2/(4\alpha t)\right)$, where $\alpha = k/(\rho c)$ is the thermal
diffusivity (m²/s). The distance at which the profile has fallen to $1/e$ of its peak is

$$
\ell = \sqrt{4\alpha t}
$$ {#eq-m27-diffusion-length}

Conduction is slow and grows only with the square root of time. This is why a lesion keeps growing
for a while after the surface has heated, and why the depth of a lesion depends on duration as well
as power.

**Key takeaways**

- Storage = conduction + RF source − perfusion; cooling at the tip enters as a boundary condition.
- At steady state $T = T_b + A/r - B/r^2$; an isotherm lesion edge scales with electrode radius.
- Heat spreads over a distance of about $\sqrt{4\alpha t}$: depth needs time.

### From temperature to injury

**A threshold temperature.** The simplest rule draws the lesion edge at one temperature. In RF
ablation models 50 °C is the most frequently used isotherm, although 48 °C and 59 °C have also been
used [@berjano2006]. One experimental basis: in isolated guinea-pig papillary muscle heated for 60 s,
excitability was lost reversibly between 42.7 and 51.3 °C and irreversibly at 50 °C or more
[@nath1993]. Tissue between those
limits can stop conducting for a while and then recover, which is one reason an acute map can
differ from a later one.

**A rate process.** Injury depends on time as well as temperature; Moritz and Henriques showed this
for skin burns [@moritz1947]. Arrhenius models, which go back to Henriques' work on burns
[@berjano2006], treat injury as a first-order reaction: the
undamaged fraction $C$ falls as $dC/dt = -k_d(T)\,C$ with rate $k_d = A\,e^{-E_a/(R T)}$, where
$A$ (1/s) and $E_a$ (J/mol) are tissue constants, $R$ is the gas constant and $T$ is in kelvin.
Integrating gives $C(t)/C_0 = e^{-\Omega(t)}$ with

$$
\Omega(t) = \int_0^{t} A\, e^{-E_a / (R\, T(\tau))}\, d\tau
$$ {#eq-m27-arrhenius}

$\Omega = 1$ leaves $1/e$ of the tissue undamaged (63 % damaged) and is a common choice for the
lesion edge. The rule has limits: at moderate hyperthermic temperatures, about 43–50 °C, Arrhenius
models often overestimate early cell death [@pearce2013]. Values of $A$ and $E_a$ for myocardium:
`TODO(source)`.

**Key takeaways**

- A threshold isotherm is simple; a 50 °C edge has an experimental basis in isolated muscle.
- The Arrhenius integral counts time at temperature; $\Omega = 1$ means 63 % damaged.
- Both are models of injury, with known limits at moderate temperatures.

### Impedance and why it falls

The generator sees one series circuit: the tip, the tissue and blood near it, the rest of the body
and the dispersive patch. Only the part near the tip changes much during an application. For a
conductivity that varies with distance, the series-shell sum from @eq-m27-spreading still holds:

$$
R_{\text{near}} = \int_{r_0}^{\infty} \frac{dr}{4\pi r^2\, \sigma\!\left(T(r)\right)}, \qquad
\sigma(T) \approx \sigma_0 \left[1 + \alpha_\sigma \left(T - T_0\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-m27-impedance}

The second part is a linear model with a temperature coefficient $\alpha_\sigma$. Most RF ablation
models use $\alpha_\sigma$ = +2 %/°C, a value measured below 42 °C [@berjano2006]; some
use other relations. Tissue conducts better as it warms, so $R_{\text{near}}$ falls as the heated zone
grows, and the shells nearest the tip count most because of the $1/r^2$ weight. This is the
physics behind the impedance drop shown during an application. In an ex vivo model, the drop in
locally measured impedance correlated with lesion size [@kawano2022].

**Key takeaways**

- Impedance falls because heated tissue conducts better, mostly in the shells next to the tip.
- The drop is an indirect sign of heating near the tip, not a measure of lesion depth.

### Lesion metrics

A mapping system can integrate what it measures during an application of length $t_a$:

$$
\text{FTI} = \int_0^{t_a} F(t)\, dt, \qquad E = \int_0^{t_a} P(t)\, dt
$$ {#eq-m27-fti}

The force–time integral (FTI, usually in g·s) counts how hard and how long the tip pressed. In a
bench model with a moving tissue contact, FTI tracked lesion size at constant power [@shah2010].
Delivered energy $E$ (J) counts generator power, not power in the tissue.

Weighted indices combine force, power and time in one number; one such index uses contact force,
time and power in a weighted formula [@das2017]. We do not reproduce commercial formulas. A generic
form is a monotone function $g$ of a weighted integral:

$$
\mathcal{I} = g\!\left(\int_0^{t_a} F(t)^{a}\, P(t)^{b}\, dt\right)
$$ {#eq-m27-weighted-index}

with exponents $a$, $b$ and the function $g$ fitted to lesion data. Every such metric leaves things
out that the derivations above say matter: how the current divides between wall and blood, how much
the tip is cooled, perfusion, wall thickness, and the time-at-temperature history. Two applications
with the same FTI can make different lesions (the tests show this for a steady and a pulsing force
trace).

**Key takeaways**

- FTI and energy are integrals of what the system measures, not of what the tissue experiences.
- Weighted indices are fitted surrogates; their weights hide model assumptions.
